subject: anhinga bird
title: This Bird's Feathers Soak Through on Purpose. Then It Spears Fish

scenes.text: This bird's feathers aren't waterproof. That's exactly how it hunts.
An anhinga's body feathers soak through the moment it dives. Add dense bones, and it sinks instead of floating.
It swims with only its head and neck above the surface. People call it the snakebird.
Underwater, a hinge in its neck snaps the bill forward like a spear and stabs the fish.
Then it surfaces, flicks the fish into the air, and swallows it headfirst.
The price is that it gets soaked and cold. So after every hunt, it stands in the sun with its wings spread wide.

description:
The anhinga's body feathers are not waterproof, and that is how it hunts.
Most water birds float. The anhinga's body plumage soaks through when it dives, and together with its dense bones that gives it neutral buoyancy, so it can swim fully submerged with only its head and neck showing, which is why it is called the snakebird. Underwater it holds its neck bent, then a hinge between the eighth and ninth neck vertebrae lets it shoot the bill forward and stab a fish; backward-slanting serrations on the bill keep the fish from sliding off. It brings the catch to the surface, tosses it and swallows it headfirst. Wet plumage loses heat quickly, so the bird then perches with its wings spread to dry and warm up. Anhingas live in warm, shallow waters from the southern United States to South America and are about 89 cm long.
Have you ever seen one drying its wings? Comment below.
